data.name: Ludu
data.detailed_description:
Ludu (« ash » in breton) is a free adventure game created with RPG Maker 2003.

You play a character living peacefully in his small house and, when he leaves home, discovers a shadow of himself and tries to follow it.
You progress through the game by solving riddles, and discover what is this strange shadow you see constantly.

Ludu won the "Bronze Alex" at the Alex d'Or 2013, and the award "Best Level-design" !

reviews.review:
Ludu is a compact adventure built around mystery, exploration, and puzzle solving rather than the combat-heavy mechanics normally associated with RPG Maker games. Developed and published by Léo-Games, it uses RPG Maker 2003 to deliver an intentionally old-school experience where curiosity is the main force pushing the player forward. Its presentation is simple and unmistakably dated, but the limited technology also gives the game a certain handmade character that suits its strange and mysterious premise.

The story begins with an ordinary situation. The protagonist is living peacefully in a small house until something unusual appears outside: a mysterious shadow that looks remarkably similar to the protagonist. Instead of providing an immediate explanation, the game encourages the player to follow this figure and discover where it leads. This simple encounter becomes the foundation of the adventure. It works because the mystery is easy to understand while leaving enough unanswered questions to encourage exploration. Even the title carries additional meaning, with “Ludu” translating to “ash” in Breton, adding another curious element to the game's identity.

Gameplay places puzzles and riddles at the center of progression. Despite being created in RPG Maker, this is not primarily an experience about gaining levels, collecting increasingly powerful equipment, or fighting endless groups of enemies. Observation and logical thinking are much more important. Players need to examine environments, understand clues, and determine how different elements relate to each other. This makes progression feel closer to an old-fashioned puzzle adventure presented through an RPG framework.

Level design is one of the more interesting aspects of the game. Locations function as more than simple pathways connecting story events because navigating and understanding them forms part of the challenge. The design encourages players to pay attention instead of simply moving toward obvious objectives. This emphasis has historical significance as well, since the game received recognition for its level design during the Alex d'Or 2013 competition, along with a Bronze Alex award. That achievement makes sense when considering how heavily the experience depends on carefully constructed environments and puzzles.

Visually, Ludu clearly reflects its RPG Maker 2003 origins. The graphics, interface, resolution, animations, and movement can feel primitive compared with modern independent games. Players who enjoy classic RPG Maker projects may find this nostalgic and charming, while newcomers could initially find the presentation restrictive. Fortunately, the mysterious atmosphere does not depend on advanced graphics. The simplicity actually allows the strange premise and puzzle construction to remain at the center of attention.

The game is also extremely lightweight. Its modest technical requirements and tiny storage footprint make it suitable for older or low-powered computers. Partial controller support is available, although the game's age and design mean keyboard controls may still provide the most straightforward experience. Being offered as a free game also makes its limited scale much easier to accept. It is not trying to provide dozens of hours of content or the mechanical complexity of a commercial role-playing epic. Instead, it offers a focused adventure that can be approached without a financial commitment.

Steam Deck compatibility is officially categorized as Playable rather than fully Verified. Performance with the default graphics configuration is considered suitable, and the game can run successfully on SteamOS. However, handheld players should expect compromises. Some functionality is not fully accessible through the default controller configuration, touchscreen interaction or a community controller layout may occasionally be useful, and text entry can require manually opening the virtual keyboard. Some interface text may also appear small, while certain prompts can display keyboard, mouse, or non-Steam Deck controller icons. It is therefore functional on the Deck, but the experience is less seamless than a fully optimized handheld release.

Its biggest weaknesses are closely connected to its age. The presentation can feel crude, modern convenience features are limited, and puzzle progression can occasionally slow dramatically when the intended solution is unclear. Players expecting extensive combat, character customization, elaborate dialogue systems, or contemporary production quality may find the experience too basic. Its strongest audience is instead composed of players who enjoy obscure indie adventures, classic RPG Maker creations, riddles, environmental puzzles, and games that prioritize ideas over technical sophistication.

Taken on those terms, Ludu is an interesting little artifact from an earlier period of independent game development. The mysterious shadow provides a straightforward reason to keep exploring, while the puzzle-oriented structure gives the journey more substance than its humble appearance initially suggests. It will not satisfy everyone, particularly those seeking a conventional RPG, but its focused design, unusual atmosphere, free availability, and emphasis on solving environmental challenges make it worth investigating for fans of retro puzzle adventures. It is modest in scale but clearly built around a specific creative idea rather than unnecessary complexity.

Rating: 7/10
